passages.t: The righteous perish unnoticed, and idols under every tree
passages.happening:
‘The righteous perish, and no one takes it to heart’ (verse 1). Devout people are swept away, and no one sees that they are spared from the evil to come. ‘Those who walk uprightly enter into peace; they find rest, lying down in death’ (verse 2).

Then God summons the idolaters. He calls them children of a sorceress and of adulterers (verse 3), people who mock and stick out their tongues (verse 4). They burn with lust under every green tree, and in the valleys they kill their children (verse 5). They pour out offerings to the smooth stones of the valley (verse 6). They have made their bed on a high hill to offer sacrifices (verse 7) and set up their memorial behind the door (verse 8). They went to Molech with oil and sent envoys far away, down even to Sheol (verse 9). They wore themselves out and never said there was no hope (verse 10).

Whom did they fear, that they lied and forgot God (verse 11)? He will expose their works, and they will not help them (verse 12). When they cry out, let their idols save them. ‘Yet the wind will carry off all of them, a breath will take them away’ (verse 13). ‘But he who seeks refuge in Me will inherit the land and possess My holy mountain’ (verse 13).
passages.hearers:
Chapter 56 ended with blind watchmen and greedy shepherds. Chapter 57 shows the result. The righteous die unnoticed, and the people turn to old idolatries. The problem that sent Israel into exile had not gone away.

The practices named here are well known from Israel's history before the exile. Second Kings 21 tells how King Manasseh, in the first half of the seventh century BC, rebuilt the high places, made his son pass through the fire and practiced sorcery. Jeremiah condemned child sacrifice in the Valley of Hinnom outside Jerusalem. Scholars disagree about when this chapter was spoken: some see an older oracle from before the exile placed here, others a word to the community after the return, among whom such practices had lingered or revived. The text does not settle it.

Canaanite worship was held at hilltop shrines and under large trees linked with fertility. The prophets often describe it in sexual terms, and many scholars have held that it included sexual rites, though how widespread they were is now debated. That explains why adultery and idolatry are mixed together here. Molech is usually read as the name of a god linked with child sacrifice, though some scholars read the word as a kind of sacrifice, or as the word for king. Sheol is the realm of the dead, and consulting the dead was forbidden to Israel. The picture is of a people reaching everywhere for security, even into the grave, and never turning to the God who made them.
passages.later: Jeremiah says of the Valley of Hinnom that God ‘never commanded, nor did it even enter My mind’ (Jeremiah 7:31). The law had told Israel to destroy the shrines ‘on the hills, and under every green tree’ (Deuteronomy 12:2).
passages.hard:
Why does the chapter use such frank sexual language for idolatry, and why is it spoken to the people as a woman?

The prophets described the covenant as a marriage, so unfaithfulness to God was called adultery (Hosea 2; Jeremiah 3; Ezekiel 16). The worship condemned here may have involved actual sexual rites, so the language may be partly literal. And the shock is meant: the prophet wants his hearers to feel the betrayal as God feels it. Some interpreters have raised concerns about how such imagery portrays women, and those concerns deserve a hearing. Others stress that the picture names the whole people, men as much as women, and that its aim is to expose betrayal, not to demean.

This is a prophetic picture of a people's unfaithfulness. It gives no warrant for any man to shame or harm a woman. And the killing of children in verse 5 is named as the evil it is; God says through Jeremiah that it never entered his mind.

If someone is hurting you, at home, at work or in a church, your safety comes first. Tell someone you trust and get help; the Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: The people wore themselves out reaching for help everywhere but God. Ask where you go first when you are afraid. And ask whose death or faithfulness around you has gone unnoticed, and whether you have taken it to heart.

passages.t: The high and holy One dwells with the contrite
passages.happening:
‘Build it up, build it up, prepare the way, take every obstacle out of the way of My people’ (verse 14).

‘For thus says the One who is high and lifted up, who inhabits eternity, whose name is Holy’ (verse 15). He dwells in a high and holy place, ‘and with the oppressed and humble in spirit, to restore the spirit of the lowly and revive the heart of the contrite’ (verse 15).

He will not accuse forever or always be angry, or the spirit of the people he made would fail (verse 16). He was angry at their greed and struck them, yet they kept going their own way (verse 17). ‘I have seen his ways, but I will heal him’ (verse 18). He will guide and comfort them and their mourners (verse 18). ‘Peace, peace to those far and near’ (verse 19), says the LORD, and he will heal them.

‘But the wicked are like the storm-tossed sea, for it cannot be still, and its waves churn up mire and muck’ (verse 20). The LORD says there is no peace for the wicked (verse 21).
passages.hearers:
The chapter turns in verse 14 with the call of 40:3, to prepare the way. Then comes one of the Bible's great pictures of God's nearness to the humble.

Verse 15 balances height and lowliness in matched lines. God is high and lifted up, and he is with the crushed. He is holy, and he revives the lowly. The word for contrite means crushed, from the same root used of the Servant crushed for the people's iniquities in chapter 53. The word for humble stands against the word for high in the same verse. The high God comes down to the low.

The word peace, shalom, frames the chapter. The righteous enter peace in death (verse 2). God promises peace to those far and near (verse 19). The doubled word means peace complete.

The last verse repeats the refrain that closed chapter 48, marking another turn in the book. The wicked are like the sea that cannot rest.
passages.later: Paul quotes verse 19 of Christ, who ‘came and preached peace to you who were far away and peace to those who were near’ (Ephesians 2:17). A psalm says the same of the contrite: ‘a broken and a contrite heart, O God, You will not despise’ (Psalm 51:17).
passages.asks: The highest God says he lives with the crushed and the lowly. Ask where in your life you feel crushed, and whether you believe God is near there. And ask what restlessness in you is like the sea that cannot be still.
